worst_places.before: React's render phase assumes it has exclusive, eventually-consistent control over the subtree it's rendering — it builds a workInProgress tree and, on a high-priority interruption, discards that in-progress work and restarts from `current` (the last committed tree), relying on the fact that nothing observable happened during the discarded render (see the discard-and-restart mechanics).
worst_places.after: React's render phase assumes it alone controls the subtree it renders, and that the subtree only has to be consistent by the end. It builds a `workInProgress` tree as it goes. Restarting is safe only because nothing observable happened during the discarded render (see the discard-and-restart mechanics).

worst_places.after:
Virtual DOM — это описание будущего UI обычными JavaScript-объектами. React строит такое описание на каждый рендер, сравнивает с предыдущим и переносит в реальный DOM только разницу.

Зачем это нужно: реальный DOM (Document Object Model — представление страницы внутри браузера) менять напрямую сравнительно медленно. Браузеру может потребоваться пересчитать layout и перерисовать экран в ответ на изменение. Если приложение делает много прямых обновлений по одному, браузер выполняет эту дорогую работу несколько раз для того, что логически является одним обновлением.

patterns: THE dominant pattern: the pyramid is present but its apex is a paragraph. In ~30 answers the first sentence really is the direct answer — and then packs the definition, the mechanism and the caveat into one dash-chained clause chain of 35-55 words in RU and 45-118 words in EN (q-7, q-10, q-17, q-19, q-37, q-39, q-48, q-71, q-74, q-78, q-82, q-83, q-98). The fix is never to cut a fact: it is to split the apex into 2-4 sentences that carry the same 3-4 facts. This one habit accounts for most of the 761 over-long-sentence flags and for the majority of the 75 'indirect lead' flags, which are not actually indirect — just too long to land.

11 of 98 answers (q-5, q-30, q-33, q-43, q-45, q-46, q-47, q-49, q-87, q-88, q-89) open directly with a 15-30 line code fence and no prose lead at all. For a phone reader in a short burst this is a full screen of scrolling before any statement of the answer. Every one of these already contains a perfectly good lead sentence — it is just sitting below the code, where it reads as commentary instead of as the answer.

Explanatory paragraphs are almost always introduced by a bold label («**Почему обычное `=` не работает:**», '**The trade-off:**', '**Что НЕ перехватывается:**'). This is a genuinely good, scannable habit and should be kept. But the label is then followed by a single 60-130-word sentence, so the scannability stops at the colon: the reader can find the paragraph they want and then still cannot read it in one pass. Labels should introduce 2-4 short sentences, not one long one.

The senior tier (q-51 through q-68) is written in a visibly different and much better register than the rest of the bank: `###` sub-headings instead of bold labels, short declarative sentences, plain hyphens, and 'Типичная ошибка на интервью' / 'Common interview trap' as the closing section. It is the most readable third of the zone at the highest difficulty level, which proves the depth is not what makes the other tiers hard. That register is the model the junior/middle/advanced tiers should be brought toward.

RU carries a recurring layer of English grammar left untranslated: «запрос в полёте» (in-flight request, 5 entries), «опаковый ID» (opaque), «рябь ре-рендеров» (ripple of re-renders), «не гоняющаяся сама с собой» (doesn't race itself), «гейтить», «репервизация», «неоформленные примитивы» (unstyled primitives), «нет хука для закрытия» (no hook for tearing down — where «хук» already means a React hook two lines earlier). Individually minor, collectively they make the RU read as a translation rather than as Russian.

Abbreviation discipline is the weakest single axis. UI is used 21-25 times and never expanded anywhere in either locale. DOM is expanded exactly once, in q-14, while 28 other uses are spread across answers a reader may open first (q-1, q-2, q-6, q-20, q-28, q-51, q-66, q-98). q-97 alone introduces ICU, CLDR, LTR, RTL and i18n and expands none of the five. Because a question bank is read out of order, 'it is expanded in another answer' does not help — each answer needs its own first-use gloss.
notes:
The script's '17 answers lack the pitfall marker' is a false positive: the whole senior tier (q-51..q-68, 18 answers) closes with «Типичная ошибка на интервью» / 'Common interview trap' instead. All 98 answers in both locales do have a closing pitfall section — the convention is consistent per tier, not missing.
Six answers contain no code block at all (q-48, q-51, q-66, q-71, q-79, q-94) and these are exactly the theory walls the script flagged; each would carry an existing-style diagram or table well — q-51 a two-tree/alternate diagram, q-58 already has an inline timeline that q-71 and q-94 could copy.
95 code lines exceed 95 characters across 53 answers (worst: q-77, q-76, q-98, q-91, q-96, q-50, q-44) — this is the only real threat to the otherwise strong E score, and it is a pure line-wrapping fix with no change to behaviour.
One technical staleness note outside the rubric: q-84 builds its Tabs on `React.cloneElement` without flagging that it is deprecated in React 19, while q-59 does correctly note the React 19 ref changes.
If the two locales were scored separately for verdict, `ru` would be targeted-fixes; `en` alone forces systemic-refactor, because 511 of its 886 sentences are over the limit and the fix is a sentence-splitting pass over every entry.
